raw_evidence.content: Three independent regime measures appear in this dataset. Polity IV ('p4v2016.csv') scores countries from -10 (full autocracy) to +10 (full democracy) along authority dimensions. The Boix-Miller-Rosato dataset ('democracy-v3.0.csv') provides a binary democracy/non-democracy classification dating back to 1800. Using three measures lets the analyst check that any 'democracy effect' isn't an artefact of how democracy is coded.

raw_evidence.label: Why The Economist's claim was contested
raw_evidence.content: The thesis — that democracies bend the epidemic curve more than autocracies — was contested on three fronts. (1) Selection: democracies that suffered the biggest outbreaks (Italy, Spain, the United States, the UK) are over-represented in the early COVID-19 data, so behavioural responses there may say more about wave severity than regime type. (2) Measurement: autocracies under-report cases and deaths, biasing direct outcome comparisons. (3) Causality: GDP per capita, state capacity, and trust in institutions are all correlated with both democracy and epidemic outcomes, so controls matter. Subsequent academic work (Annaka 2021; Cepaluni, Dorsch & Branyiczki 2022) has produced both supportive and qualifying findings.

raw_evidence.content: If democracies really do contain epidemics better, it pushes back on a long-standing political-science argument that autocracies are more 'efficient' in crises. It also has direct policy implications: the question is not 'how strict was the lockdown?' but 'how much did people actually move less?' — i.e. compliance, which depends on trust between citizens and the state. Subsequent excess-mortality estimates (e.g. The Economist's own model and IHME) reinforced the picture that the early-pandemic gap between regimes was real, even if narrower than initially claimed.
